content:
You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`. You cannot read or search the files either: subagents read the code for you, so ask them for what you need to know.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /luxon.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Your attention is the scarce resource: while your own tools run, new requests wait until they finish. Subagents run in the background, so delegate long work (investigating and fixing a bug, running a test suite) and keep yourself free to respond to new requests and to combine reports.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

## Accessors

Luxon DateTimes have a few different accessors that let you find out about the zone and offset:

```js
var dt = DateTime.local();

dt.zoneName; //=> 'America/New_York'
dt.offset; //=> -240
dt.offsetNameShort; //=> 'EDT'
dt.offsetNameLong; //=> 'Eastern Daylight Time'
dt.isOffsetFixed; //=> false
dt.isInDST; //=> true
```

Those are all documented in the [DateTime API docs](../class/src/datetime.js~DateTime.html).

## DST weirdness

Because our ancestors were morons, they opted for a system wherein many governments shift around the local time twice a year for no good reason. And it's not like they do it in a neat, coordinated fashion. No, they do it whimsically, varying the shifts' timing from country to country (or region to region!) and from year to year. And of course, they do it the opposite way south of the Equator. This is all a tremendous waste of everyone's energy and, er, time, but it is how the world works and a date and a time library has to deal with it.

Most of the time, DST shifts will happen without you having to do anything about it and everything will just work. Luxon goes to some pains to make DSTs as unweird as possible. But there are exceptions. This section covers them.

195	But how do those conversions actually work? First, uncontroversially:
   196	
   197	 * 1 week = 7 days
   198	 * 1 day = 24 hours
   199	 * 1 hour = 60 minutes
   200	 * 1 minute = 60 seconds
   201	 * 1 second = 1000 milliseconds
   202	 
   203	These are always true and you can roll them up and down with consistency (e.g. `1 hour = 60 * 60 * 1000 milliseconds`). However, this isn't really true for the higher order units, which vary in length, even putting DSTs aside. A year is sometimes 365 days long and sometimes 366. Months are 28, 29, 30, or 31 days. By default Luxon converts between these units using what you might call "casual" conversions:
   204	
   205	|         | Month | Week | Day |
   206	| ---     | ---   |  --- | --- |
   207	| Year    | 12    |   52 | 365 |
   208	| Quarter | 3     |   13 |  91 |
   209	| Month   |       |    4 |  30 |
   210	
   211	These should match your intuition and for most purposes they work well. But they're not just wrong; they're not even self-consistent:
   212	
   213	```js
   214	dur.shiftTo('months').shiftTo('days').as('years') //=> 0.9863013698630136
   215	```
   216	
   217	This is because 12 * 30 != 365. These errors can be annoying, but they can also cause significant issues if the errors accumulate:
   218	
   219	```js
   220	var dur = Duration.fromObject({ years: 50000 });
   221	DateTime.local().plus(dur.shiftTo('milliseconds')).year //=> 51984
   222	DateTime.local().plus(dur).year                         //=> 52017
   223	```
   224	
   225	Those are 33 years apart! So Luxon offers an alternative conversion scheme called "longterm", based on the 400-year calendar cycle:
   226	
   227	|         | Month |     Week |       Day |
   228	|----     | ---   |      --- |       --- |
   229	| Year    | 12    |  52.1775 |  365.2425 |
   230	| Quarter |  3    | 13.04435 | 91.310625 |
   231	| Month   |       | 4.348125 | 30.436875 |
   232	
   233	You can see why these are irritating to work with, which is why they're not the default.
   234	
   235	Luxon methods that create Durations de novo accept an option called `conversionAccuracy`. You can set it to "casual" or "longterm". It's a property of the Duration itself, so any conversions you do use the rule you've picked, and any new Durations you derive from it will retain that property.
   236	
   237	```js
   238	Duration.fromObject({ years: 23, conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });
   239	Duration.fromISO('PY23', { conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });
   240	
   241	end.diff(start, 'days', { conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' })
   242	```
   243	
   244	You can also create an accurate Duration out of an existing one:
   245	
   246	```js
   247	var pedanticDuration = casualDuration.reconfigure({ conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });
   248	```
   249	
   250	These Durations will do their conversions differently.
   251	
   252	
   253	### Losing information
   254	
   255	Be careful of converting between units. It's easy to lose information. Let's say we converted a diff into days:
   256	
   257	
   258	```js
   259	var end = DateTime.fromISO('2017-03-13');
   260	var start = DateTime.fromISO('2017-02-13');
   261	diffInMonths.as('days'); //=> 30
   262	```
   263	
   264	That's our conversion between months and days (you could also do a longterm-accurate conversion; it wouldn't fix the issue ahead). But this isn't the number of days between February 15 and March 15!
   265	
   266	```js
   267	var diffInDays = end.diff(start, 'days');
   268	diffInDays.toObject(); //=> { days: 28 }
   269	```
   270	
   271	It's important to remember that diffs are Duration objects, and a Duration is just a dumb pile of time units our computation spat out. Unlike an Interval, a Duration doesn't "remember" what the inputs to the diff were. So we lost some information converting between units. This mistake is really common when rolling up:
   272	
   273	
   274	```js
   275	var diff = end.diff(start) // default unit is milliseconds
   276	
   277	// wtf, that's not a month!
   278	diff.as('months'); //=> 0.9319444 
   279	
   280	// it's not even the right number of days! (hint: my time zone has a DST)
   281	diff.shiftTo('hours').as('days'); //=> 27.958333333333332
   282	```
   283	
   284	Normally you won't run into this problem if you think clearly about what you want to do with a diff. But sometimes you really do want an object that represents the subtraction itself, not the result. [Intervals](../class/src/interval.js~Interval.html) can help. Intervals are mostly used to keep track of ranges of time, but they make for "anchored" diffs too. For example:
   285	
   286	```js
   287	var end = DateTime.fromISO('2017-03-13');
   288	var start = DateTime.fromISO('2017-02-13');
   289	var i = Interval.fromDateTimes(start, end);
   290	
   291	i.length('days');       //=> 28
   292	i.length('months')      //=> 1
   293	```
   294	
   295	Because the Interval stores its endpoints and computes `length` on the fly, it retakes the diff each time you query it. Of course, precisely because an Interval *isn't* an abstract bundle of time, it can't be used in places where Durations can. For example, you can't add them to DateTime via `plus()` because Luxon wouldn't know what units to do the math in (see "Calendar vs time math" above). But you can convert the interval into a Duration by picking the units:
   296	
   297	```js
   298	i.toDuration('months').toObject(); //=> { months: 1 }
   299	i.toDuration('days').toObject(); //=> { days: 28 }
   300	```
   301	
   302	You can even pick multiple units:
   303	
   304	```js
   305	end = DateTime.fromISO('2018-05-25');
   306	i = start.until(end);
   307	i.toDuration(['years', 'months', 'days']).toObject(); //=> { years: 1, months: 3, days: 12 }
   308	```

arguments.report:
## Bug & fix

**Root cause:** `padStart(input, n)` in `/luxon/src/impl/util.js` padded the *whole stringified number* including its sign:
```js
return ("0".repeat(n) + input).slice(-n);   // padStart(-5, 4) => "00-5"
```
`DateTime#toISODate()` renders `yyyy` via `Formatter.num(dt.year, 4)` → `padStart(year, 4)` (forceSimple path in `src/impl/formatter.js`), so negative years with fewer than 4 digits were mangled (`-5` → `"00-5-01-01"`, `-100` → `"-100-01-01"`).

**Fix applied (only file edited: `/luxon/src/impl/util.js`):**
```diff
 export function padStart(input, n = 2) {
-  if (input.toString().length < n) {
-    return ("0".repeat(n) + input).slice(-n);
-  } else {
-    return input.toString();
-  }
+  const isNeg = input < 0,
+    str = (isNeg ? -input : input).toString(),
+    padded = str.length < n ? ("0".repeat(n) + str).slice(-n) : str;
+  return isNeg ? "-" + padded : padded;
 }
```
Sign is stripped, the magnitude is zero-padded to `n`, then the sign is re-attached. Kept the existing repeat/slice style (no native `String.padStart`, for old-runtime compatibility). The pre-existing `objToLocalTS` change (year-2000 leap-year comment) was left untouched, as were `src/interval.js` and `src/datetime.js`.

## Verification

1. **Required jest command:** `test/datetime/iso.test.js` **does not exist in this repo** — the ISO tests live in `test/datetime/format.test.js`. Ran `npx jest test/datetime/format.test.js test/impl`: **2 suites, 72/72 passed**. (Running the literal `npx jest test/datetime/iso.test.js test/impl` silently runs only `test/impl`, 13/13 passed.)

2. **/tmp script** (`/tmp/verify_iso.js`, run via `npx babel-node`) — all required cases PASS:
   - `year -5` → `"-0005-01-01"` ✓
   - `year -100, month 12, day 31` → `"-0100-12-31"` ✓
   - `year -12345` → `"-12345-01-01"` ✓
   - `year 5` → `"0005-01-01"` ✓

-    return input.toString();

        weeks: 52,
        days: 365,
        hours: 365 * 24,

        seconds: 365 * 24 * 60 * 60,
        milliseconds: 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000
      },
